When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a written record of what Dimna had said in his defense <note>original: "ma'adhirihi"</note>. The Lion took the document and ordered them to withdraw.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I am harsh with you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that as long as you continue to delay your decision regarding Dimna's case, he will stir up against you troubles that you will be unable to withstand or overcome."

Then she stood up and left in anger. On the following day, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after the accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. By doing so, you would save your soul from the consequences of the afterlife, and a good reputation would return to you for two reasons: first, your ability to find ways out and fabricate excuses <note>original: "ma'adhir"</note> to defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in a state of beauty is better than life in a state of ugliness."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not rule based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself best, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty beyond doubt. My case has only become ugly in your eyes because you have suspected that I acted with malice."

Whoever is a slave to greed,
How can his eye and heart become bright?
Whoever possesses greed finds no purity;
The eye of the heart is not illuminated by greed.
Before his eyes, the vision of status and gold
Is just like a hair within the eye. <note>original: "بوی" (hair/fiber) in the OCR, likely "موی" in the Persian text, referring to a physical obstruction in the eye.</note>
The thought of status and gold, to the greedy,
Is like a hair or a thorn in the eye.
Except perhaps for the drunkard who is full of God;
Though he be in a corner, he is a secret treasure.
The one drunk on the love of Truth is full of the Beloved;
If you give him a treasure-house, he remains in that state.
Whoever has been blessed by the Vision <note>The spiritual sight of God.</note>
This world becomes like a carcass in his eyes.
Whoever is blessed by the Vision,
This world becomes a carcass to his sight.
But that Sufi was far from such intoxication;
Inevitably, in his greed, he was night-blind.
Whoever is far from this drunken state,
That pseudo-Sufi becomes night-blind through greed.
The ear of greed may hear a hundred stories,
Yet not a single point enters the ear of greed.
Though the greedy listen to a hundred tales,
The ear of their intellect takes no share of it.

There was a certain bankrupt man, homeless,
Languishing in prison and in merciless bonds.
There was a homeless bankrupt man,
Who could find no release from the bonds of prison.
He ate the morsels of the prisoners excessively;
To the hearts of the people, his greed was like Mount Qaf.
He was a free-loader of the prisoners' morsels;
The mountain of his greed was a burden on the hearts of the people.
No one had the courage to eat a morsel of bread,
Because that snatcher of morsels would carry it away.
No one had the soul to eat a morsel of bread;
He would stretch out his hand in greed immediately.
Whoever is far from the invitation of the Compassionate One,
He is a beggar even if he be a Sultan.
Whoever lacks the grace of God’s success,
He is a beggar in his eyes, even if he were a King.
He had set aside manliness for the sake of that theft;
He became a prisoner of hell because of that bread-snatching.
He set aside virtue for that theft,
And became a prisoner of hell, a snatcher of bread.
If you turn your ear toward the hope of comfort,
An affliction will surely come from that side as well.
In the hope of a corner of comfort,
There is certainly an affliction from one side.
There is no treasure without a trap and a snare;
There is no rest except in the private chamber of God.
There is no corner that is not a trapping-ground;
The private chamber of God is the only true refuge.
The corner of the prison of this world, inevitably,
Is not without its price and the beating of the mat. <note>A reference to the hardships and punishments of prison life.</note>
The corner of the prison of the world is full of types of cruelty;
It has become a place of suffering and various hardships.
By God, even if you enter a mouse hole,
You will be afflicted by the claws of a cat.
Even if your place were a mouse hole,
The cat's claws would make you drink the poison of death.
The human being is made of imagination;
If his imagination is beautiful, he is beautiful.
Man finds consolation in imagination;
If his imaginations are pleasant, he has a beautiful state.
If unpleasantness appears in his imagination,
He melts like wax from the heat of a fire.
If long, terrifying imaginations occur,
The soul melts like wax in the fire.
If God keeps you amidst snakes and scorpions
With pleasant imaginations,
If in the midst of snakes and scorpions your imagination
Is a good thought through the help of the Lord of Majesty,
The snakes and scorpions will be your companions,
Because your imagination is the alchemy of copper. <note>Turning the "copper" of hardship into the "gold" of spiritual comfort.</note>
The snakes and scorpions become companions to that person,
Whose imagination is the alchemy of copper.
Sweet patience comes to you from a pleasant imagination,
Because that imagination of relief has come before you.
Show sweet patience through a beautiful imagination,
For relief is the description of the state that lies ahead.
That relief comes from faith in the heart;
Weakness of faith is despair and groaning.
The image of relief is in the heart through faith;
Know that weakness of faith is despair and distress.
Patience stands as the head and crown of faith;
As it is said: "Where there is no patience, there is no faith."
Patience is the crown of perfect faith;
Whoever lacks patience and endurance is not complete.
The Prophet said: "God has not given faith
To anyone who has no patience in his nature."
The Prophet said that perfect faith
Is not found in one who lacks patience.
That one thing may be like a snake in your eye,
While in the eye of another, it is a beautiful image.
In your eye, that imagination is a snake;
In the other's eye, it has become a beautiful state.
Because in your eye is the imagination of infidelity,
While that is the imagination of a believer in the eye of a friend.
Infidelity is there because your imagination is dark;
Sometimes it is a hook, and sometimes it is a fish.
For in this part, both actions exist;
Sometimes it is a fish, and sometimes it is a hook.
In a single person, two forms are manifest:
Half is greed, and half is the quality of the patient.
Half of him is a believer, half is infidelity;
Half of him brings greed, half of him is patience.
Half is a believer, half is the image of an infidel;
Half is greed, and half is the quality of the patient.
Your Lord said: "Among you is the believer,"
And also: "Among you is the ancient infidelity of the infidel."
The Truth said: "Among you are infidels,"
And also said: "Among you are believers."

A clamor arose throughout the entire city,
The anxiety in the heart of that Sultan increased.
The hearts of the common and elite of the city were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.
Is a powerful enemy intending to attack us?
Or has a calamity of the kingdom arisen from the Unseen?
For Dalqak <note>a famous court jester</note> has arrived in great haste,
And killed several Arabian horses along the road.
The people gathered at the King's palace,
Asking why he arrived with such frantic speed.
From his haste, a great commotion of effort arose,
A tumult and agitation spread through the city of Termez.
One person was raising both hands in prayer,
While another, out of anxiety, was wailing "Alas!"
From the outcry, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart was filled with a hundred kinds of imaginings.
Everyone made a prediction based on their own conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the wool.
The King quickly sought a path and gave him entry;
When he kissed the ground, the King said: "Hey, what happened?"
To whoever asked him of his condition, that sour-faced man
Put his finger to his lips, saying: "Hush!"
His cleverness only inflamed the King's imagination,
And everyone became stunned and confused by his agitation.
Dalqak signaled: "O Munificent King,
Leave me for a moment so I may catch my breath,
Until my fleeting intellect returns to me,
For I have fallen into a wondrous world."
After an hour, when the King was consumed by suspicion and doubt,
Both his throat and his mouth turned bitter.
For he had never seen Dalqak in such a state;
There was no companion more pleasant than him.
He used to always practice trickery and jesting,
Keeping the King happy and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in his seat
That the King would clutch his stomach from the pressure.
His body would break into a sweat from the force of laughter,
And he would fall on his face from the intensity of it.
Yet today he is so pale and sour-faced,
Putting his finger to his lips, saying: "O King, be silent!"
Doubt upon doubt and fantasy upon fantasy arose,
Wondering what punishment would befall the King.
For the King's heart was filled with grief and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings of that region,
Either by guile or by the power of that stubborn one.
This King of Termez was in a state of fearful imagination,
And that imagination increased because of Dalqak's trickery.
He said: "Speak quickly! What is the situation?
From whom is this turmoil and agitation of yours?"
He replied: "I heard in the village that the King
Has sent a herald to every crossroads,
Saying: 'I want someone who, in three days,
Can reach Samarkand, and if he succeeds,
I have set aside treasures for him in exchange.'
When the purpose of the message is achieved,
I hurried there for that reason,
To say that I do not have that ability!
Such a lowly task does not suit one like me;
Do not weave the thread of this hope upon me."

When the King had finished with the delicious morsels, he set the wine in motion and arranged a banquet of joy.
When the King had drunk two or three goblets of wine, the sweat of heat rose from his rose-colored face.
He said, "O host of the golden palace, your place is pleasant and your provisions are ample.
But these sixty steps of the high palace, which the sky itself would need a lasso to reach,
How can you, after sixty years have passed over you, traverse them beneath your feet?"
The host said, "May the King remain eternal; may his wine be from <term>Kawsar</term> <gloss>a river in Paradise</gloss> and his cupbearer a <term>Houri</term> <gloss>a maiden of Paradise</gloss>.
This is not a marvel from me, for I am a man; how could I be exhausted by such a staircase?
The marvel is that there is a daughter like the moon, soft and delicate like the King's silk and ermine.
She takes a cow, heavy as a mountain, upon her neck and brings it to the place where it eats its fodder.
She carries it up the sixty steps in one go, such that she does not stop to rest on any step.
And what a cow! A cow like an elephant, which cannot move its own fat a single inch.
By God, if anyone in this land could even lift its breath from the ground!
Yet a woman carries it up a sixty-step fortress; how can this work not be a wonder?"
When the colonel told this story to the King, the King pressed his fingertip beneath his teeth in amazement.
He said, "How can a deed of this kind be? It cannot be, and if it is, it must be sorcery.
I will not believe this speech to be true until I first see it with my own eyes."
Then he requested of the host that he make the claim of his speech come true.
When the host heard this, he went down and told the lion's tale to the cow-carrier <note>The "lion" refers to the King, and the "cow-carrier" refers to Fitna, the slave girl</note>.

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> left the corner of the monastery and sat at the foot of the wine-vat,
Ever since he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>moral police officer</gloss> carrying a jug of wine on his shoulder.

The state of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>elder</gloss>, the <term>Qazi</term> <gloss>judge</gloss>, and the secret drinking of the Jews,
I asked about these at dawn from the old wine-seller.

He said: "These matters are not to be spoken of, even if you are a confidant;
Draw in your tongue, keep the veil drawn, and drink your wine."

O <term>Saqi</term> <gloss>wine-bearer</gloss>, spring is arriving and the means for wine are gone;
Think of something, for the heart's blood boils over with grief.

Your love, my poverty, youth, and the new spring;
Accept my excuse and cover my crime with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you display your eloquence like a candle?
The moth of your desire has arrived; O lover, be silent.

O King of form and meaning, the likes of whom
No eye has ever seen and no ear has ever heard.

Remain so long that your youthful fortune
May force the aged sky to accept your blue <term>khirqa</term> <gloss>dervish robe</gloss>.

Last night, a sharp-witted man of experience told me in secret,
That which should not be kept hidden from you by the wine-seller:

He said: "Take matters easily upon yourself, for by its nature,
The world treats those who strive too hard with great severity."

And then he gave me a cup, from whose radiance in the heavens,
Venus began to dance and the lute-player covered her ears in awe.

Come with a bleeding heart but a smiling lip like the wine-cup;
Do not wail like the harp if you receive a wound.

Until you become an initiate, you will not hear a secret from behind this veil;
The ear of the stranger is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the divine messenger angel</gloss>.

For a king, at the time of turning the reins,
Victory cannot be achieved through theft <note>meaning: through deception or stealth rather than open combat</note>.
Another researcher began to speak,
Saying that Dara has prepared such a vast force,
That it can only be counted by estimation,
By those who are experts in assessing armies.
Iskandar said to him: "A single sharp blade
Can cut the fat of a hundred oxen into tiny pieces." <note>original: "one sword of fat and grease shreds a hundred fattened cows." This is a metaphor for a small, sharp force overcoming a large, sluggish one.</note>
Such a worthy answer to the army
Came forth from the exalted sovereign.
The news grew more intense every moment,
That a roaring dragon was coming toward Rome.
When Iskandar realized that fierce cloud <note>original: "tund migh," referring to Dara as a storm cloud</note>
Was rarely drawing the lightning of his sword,
He sent word so that armies from every land
Should set out toward the threshold of the sovereign.
From Egypt, from Africa, Rome, and Russia,
An army was adorned like a bride.
When the boundless army became a multitude,
He requested a count of the famous heroes.
The muster-master <term>Arid</term> <gloss>an official who reviews and counts the troops</gloss> reported that three hundred thousand
Brave, solitary horsemen had come forth.
When the preparation of the army was complete,
He held a gathering outside with the wine-cup.
The wise minds of Rome sat together;
They softened their hearts like wax to the King's seal <note>meaning: they became fully obedient to his command</note>.
The King spoke of the affairs of Dara and his actions;
He spoke and pondered deeply upon his work.

<column-break/>

<note>
1. That is, one sword can shred the fat and grease of a hundred fattened cows. Variant: "can shred the hides of a hundred cows" or "the backs of a hundred cows."
2. That is, when Iskandar realized that Dara is a fierce cloud who, with the roar of thunder, draws the lightning of his sword toward him.
3. That is, the presenter and military scribe reported that three hundred thousand single horsemen were gathered. A "solitary horseman" <term>mufrad savār</term> refers to a peerless and incomparable hero. Variant: "six hundred thousand."
4. That is, by the seal of Iskandar's command, they softened the wax of their hearts and became receptive to his order. Soft wax receives an impression more quickly than hard wax.
</note>

# The Nahid Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent to seek hospitality from its people. A man with a parched complexion came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted an enemy <note>meaning food, as hunger is the enemy</note> for three days." He said: "Step aside." Then he said: "O youths, what do you think of a portion of <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and dried curd</gloss> as white as a bald man's pate, in a wide bowl, crowned with the choice froth from the sides of a great, sturdy camel, a single serving of which fills the mouth? It is for a group of famished, thirsty men who have traveled five days; the tooth disappears into it, and its pits are like the tongues of birds. They gulp down the <term>nahida</term> with bowls of milk they have milked from old, sturdy, well-fed camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread like pieces of silver ingots, arranged on a leather mat smelling of mimosa bark? A bright, clever, and nimble youth leaps to it, kneading it without shaking or rattling it. He makes it softer than a gentle king, then moistens it with milk or a heavy pestle. Then he turns to it, twists it, and leaves it in the corner of a stone oven until it thickens without becoming hard. He goes to the <term>ghada</term> wood and ignites the fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its bed of embers, then takes his dough and throws it in after perfecting its color. He spreads it out, covers it, and when it has puffed and risen, he heaps upon it glowing stones until the two heats meet. When he covers them on the matching embers with a lid, and it splits open clearly, its crust resembling thin parchment, and its redness like the red of the Hijazi dates known as 'Mother of Locusts' or 'Ibn Tab's cluster,' he pours over it white honey like snow until it sinks into the crevices of the fat, and the heart of the bread drinks what is upon it of honey. I present it to you, and you swallow it in great gulps. Do you desire it, O youths?"

He said: Each of us craned our necks at his description, our mouths watering, smacking our lips and tasting the air. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle, by God, does not hate it!" Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of a young she-goat from Najd, high-bred and wild, that has eaten the mimosa buds, the Najdi wormwood, the yarrow, and the dry herbage? She has sipped the spring water and filled herself from the lush pastures until her flanks are heavy. She is slaughtered in joy, then inverted in a pit-oven until she is cooked through without being scorched or underdone. Then we present her to you, her skin covering white fat, on a table arranged with thin loaves like spreading fine Egyptian linen or dyed cloth. She is surrounded by small bowls containing various sauces and dips. She is placed before you, dripping with fat and oozing with broth. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" He said: "And your uncle, by God, dances for it!" At this, one of us leaped at him with a sword and said: "What..."

At that point, we saw ourselves as worthy of composing words that might be transmitted from us. It became necessary for us to make you the first person to receive what we possess and to be informed of what we have attained, due to your sincere friendship and the purity of your character. However, if we were to present you with the ultimate conclusions we have reached before establishing the foundational principles with you, it would benefit you no more than a general, traditional acceptance. This would only occur if you thought well of us based on our mutual affection and friendship, rather than because we deserve to have our words accepted. We do not desire for you anything less than the highest rank, nor are we satisfied for you to remain at a level that does not guarantee salvation, let alone the attainment of the highest degrees of success.

Rather, we wish to lead you along the paths that our own journey preceded, and to have you swim in the sea that we crossed first, until it brings you to the same destination we reached. Thus, you may witness what we witnessed, realize through your own inner vision everything we realized, and become independent of tying your knowledge to what we have known. You set the share as one hundred and nine parts, then multiply thirteen by one hundred and nine parts and add eighty parts to that. This results in one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is to establish the <term>faridah</term> <gloss>legal distribution of inheritance</gloss> from twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. This is equivalent to one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate then equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, leaving five-eighths of the estate equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Thus, the entire estate equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. The estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only taken from the third.

<meta>continues from previous page: As for the error that occurs from someone other than this class of people, it is pure sin, whether the error is in theoretical or practical matters. Just as an ignorant judge who is unfamiliar with the</meta> <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>the traditions and practices of the Prophet</gloss> is not excused if he errs in a ruling, so too the one who judges concerning existing things is not excused if the conditions for judgment are not met in him. Rather, he is either a sinner or an infidel. If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the means of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him—which is the knowledge of the <term>usul</term> <gloss>fundamentals</gloss> and the knowledge of <term>istinbat</term> <gloss>deduction</gloss> from those fundamentals by <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>—how much more so should this be required for the one who judges existing things? By this I mean that he must know the rational first principles and the method of deduction from them.

In short, error regarding the Law is of two kinds. First, there is an error for which a person is excused if they are among those qualified to investigate the matter in which the error occurred, just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, or a skilled judge is excused if he errs in a ruling; however, one who is not an expert in that field is not excused. Second, there is an error for which no one is excused. If such an error occurs regarding the principles of the Law, it is <term>kufr</term> <gloss>infidelity or unbelief</gloss>, and if it occurs in what follows the principles, it is <term>bid'ah</term> <gloss>innovation</gloss>. This type of error concerns things that all classes of argumentative methods lead to knowing, such that knowledge of that thing is possible for everyone. Examples of this include the acknowledgment of God, Blessed and Exalted is He, of the prophecies, and of the happiness or misery of the afterlife. This is because these three foundations are reached through the three types of evidence which <note>The three types of evidence refer to the demonstrative, dialectical, and rhetorical methods mentioned earlier in the text.</note>

Its Sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>the name is pronounced with a short 'a' sound on the Qaf and the Ra</note>. Before his time, it belonged to Ashqiya Musa, who surrendered it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for a compensation. Al-Nasir sent a governor and an army to the city, but later Sultan Badr al-Din seized control of it and built his royal residence there, establishing his rule firmly. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my animal for him, so he dismounted from his animal and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his action and increase their honor toward him; however, if he greets them while remaining mounted, they take offense and are displeased, which often leads to the traveler being deprived of their favor. This happened to me with one of them, and I regretted it. When I had greeted him and remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be given the finest lodging. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets in silver trays, along with candles and robes of honor. He provided me with a mount and treated me excellently. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aqsaray <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the Alif, a silent Qaf, and a short 'a' on the Sad and Ra</note>.

It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities of the lands of <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through the houses. It contains many trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens within its walls. The famous carpets named after the city are manufactured there from sheep's wool; they have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Ilkhanid Mongol ruler</note>. I stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>hospice</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, the deputy there for Emir Arta. Arta is the deputy of the King of Iraq over the conquered lands of Rum. This Sharif is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>members of the youth guilds</gloss> and has a large following. He showed us complete hospitality and performed the same generous deeds as those before him.

Then we traveled to the city of Niğde <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the Nun, a silent Kaf, and a short 'a' on the Dal</note>. It is one of the cities belonging to the King of Iraq. It is a heavily populated city, though some parts of it are in ruins. It is bisected by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the great rivers. It has three bridges, one inside the city and two outside. There are waterwheels both inside and outside the city to irrigate the orchards. Fruits there are abundant. I stayed at the hospice of the <term>Fata</term> <gloss>guild member</gloss> Akhi Jaruq, who is the governor there. He honored us according to the custom of the <term>Fityan</term>. We stayed there for three days, then traveled after that to the city of Kayseri, which is one of the lands of the King of Iraq. It is one of...

Under the compulsion of necessity, an art was finally invented by which he might pay the penalty for so much blood; having investigated the narrow paths of the trails by which he was accustomed to go out at night from the shelters of the caves for prey, a path was cut. Having dug a pit and covered it with hurdles and thrown earth, with the <margin>Something about the tiger.</margin> extra earth dispersed, they finished it. The male tiger, indeed, came along incautiously, fell into the pit, and became stuck on sharp stakes fixed at the bottom of the ditch. With his roaring, he deafened the whole neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that shrieking. He was killed by casting down huge stones from the edges of the pit onto the stakes fixed in him. He broke into a thousand splinters and a thousand pieces the spears held in right hands and those hurled from above. Even half-dead and bloodless, he filled the onlookers with dread; what might he have done if free and unharmed? A certain Juan Ledesma of Seville, a friend of Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> and a companion in his labors, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than beef. When asked why they call it a tiger, those who have now seen the tiger respond that they judge it to be a tiger from its spots, its ferocity, its dexterity, and other signs given by authors. Since many of them claim to have seen both leopards and panthers, which are also spotted. After the male tiger was killed, they followed his tracks toward the mountains and reached the cave that was his conjugal home.

While the mother was absent, they carried off two cubs that were not yet old enough for their mother's teats. Changing their plan so that they might later send them to Spain once they had grown larger, they carefully fitted iron chains around their necks and brought the little ones back to the maternal cave. The "three bodies" <note>the three kayas: Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, and Nirmanakaya</note> refers to the meaning of "complete knowledge."

To show the logic of the locations connected to the positions of the body, the text says "without exception" and so forth. The phrase "in which" refers to the place of birth. The "subject matter" refers to that which is to be thoroughly taught. The phrase "in that" refers to transformation. Because there is a shared quality of creating emanations, it is called "emanation" <note>Nirmanakaya</note>. Furthermore, because the Buddhas remain in the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Emanation Body</gloss> for as long as cyclic existence lasts, its location is stable. Therefore, because there is a shared quality of being stable, the place of birth is also called "the stable place." For this reason, it is said: "by what and for what reason it is produced."

Regarding "Dharma," all phenomena <note>dharmas</note> are mind-only. Therefore, the location of the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> is the mind, because it is the foundation. Regarding "certainly enjoying the food," "food" refers to that which is utilized. The phrase "the tastes" should be connected with "at the throat." Because the enjoyment is similar, it is called the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss>. Furthermore, if one asks what the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> is, it is the teaching of the secret Dharma to the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>awakening beings</gloss>. "Great Bliss" refers to the <term>Mahasukhakaya</term> <gloss>Great Bliss Body</gloss>. "At the crown" refers to its location on the head.

In that way, just as the four <term>chakras</term> are contained within the bodies, the results and the classes are also contained; to establish this, the text says "E-Vam" and so forth. The "aspect of E-Vam" refers to the <term>chakra</term> of the place of birth. What is there? The text says "the result of similarity," which is the fruit. The <term>Dharma-chakra</term> <gloss>Dharma wheel/center</gloss> is the "maturation result." The <term>Enjoyment-chakra</term> is the "man-made result." The <term>Great Bliss-chakra</term> refers to the "stainless result." Who is—

The second <note>point</note> is whether this essence, or perhaps something even more supreme than that, is called Body, Speech, and Mind. The third <note>point</note> is: "What is the name of this venerable one?" To clarify these concepts, it is said: "How wonderful!" <note>original: "Emaho"</note> and so forth. At the end of this phrase, one should take the word "this" from the previous statement and apply it here to understand its own meaning; "this too" means "even something like this." Even if the word "this" is absent in some <note>versions of the text</note>, it should be understood as being there in meaning.

"How wonderful, Vajra Essence!" <note>original: "Emaho Vajragarbha"</note> means that all Bodhisattvas are the <term>Tathagatagarbha</term> <gloss>Essence of the One Gone to Bliss</gloss> and the <term>Tathagata-gotra</term> <gloss>Buddha Family</gloss>. Ignorance, hatred, pride, desire, and jealousy are the five Buddha families. Among these, that which is characterized by hatred is the Vajra Essence <note>Vajragarbha</note>. This Bodhisattva's name is consistent with its meaning. It is difficult to find a family of Bodhisattvas such as this. Because of the wonder born from that very fact, he is addressed as "How wonderful!"

"That Essence, Bodhisattva, Great Being, excellent, excellent!" <note>original: "Sadhu, sadhu"</note> means that the very intention to benefit others through methods such as extreme wrath is Great Compassion. Furthermore, the enlightenment that possesses the accomplishment of various purposes without a fixed time is Great Enlightenment. One who perfectly contemplates this is a Great Being <note>Mahasattva</note>. One who possesses such an intention to benefit others and an intention to benefit oneself is the supreme of persons. For that reason, the word "excellent" is repeated twice.

"Listen!" means to apply oneself to hearing. This shows that a holy person with such a family and such an intention is fortunate in this regard. If one asks how this family is to be known, it is through the signs of the particular qualities of faith and desire. As it says in the *Noble Descent into Lanka Scripture* <note>original: "Arya-Lankavatara-sutra"</note>:

By smoke, fire is known;
By the water-crane, water is known.

It emphasizes the Great Compassion and Great Enlightenment required to benefit others through various skillful means.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>conduct. Being filled by that means being satisfied in each moment together with the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to awakening</gloss>. Because that never perishes, it arises continuously and revolves; this is the meaning of "always arising." Not perishing means an uninterrupted stream that occurs constantly.

In that way, in the perfectly pure Buddha fields, one is supported by the joy and bliss of the taste of the Great Dharma. This is not like sentient beings who live on coarse food and such. If one asks what this satisfaction by the taste of Great Wisdom is, it is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss> of the Buddhas. That body is called a "Great Being" <note>original: "Mahasattva"</note>. How so? One who stays and remains, abiding without perishing, is a "Being" <note>original: "Sattva"</note>. Because he is both a being and great, he is a "Great Being," meaning he is utterly imperishable.

Regarding the phrase "always" and so forth: here, the word <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond or commitment</gloss> should be viewed as the "Great Samaya." The word indicates one aspect of the whole, just as when one mentions "Vajrabhairava," the entire host of Bhairava is understood. Because he pervades everywhere through the application of joyful activity, he is the <term>Samaya</term>. To go toward beings through various skillful means according to the inclinations of those to be trained is the "Great Samaya." A being characterized by the Great Samaya is a "Great Samaya Being" <note>original: "Mahasamayasattva"</note>.

A "Being" <note>Sattva</note> is so called because of always entering <note>The text provides an etymological derivation based on the Sanskrit roots "satata" (always) and "pravrtta" (engaged/entering)</note>. By taking the "sa" from <term>satata</term> and the "va" from <term>pravrtta</term> and removing the remainder, the term is defined. Thus it is said: "always entering." Because the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Emanation Bodies</gloss> of the Buddhas are permanent in their continuity through infinite divisions, they are "permanent." This is the meaning expressed by the term "Great Samaya."

For example, when a fire burns in a great wilderness, some parts spread, some blaze, and some go out. Similarly, the Emanation Bodies of the Buddhas show themselves being born in other Buddha fields; having been born in one place, they show themselves passing into <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>final liberation</gloss> in another place. Thus, all the world realms are never empty of them.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the path that serves as the antidote to all obscurations, the <term>paramita</term> <gloss>perfection</gloss>, will arise. Through that antidote, the latent tendencies of the phenomena associated with the afflictions accumulated in the <term>alayavijnana</term> <gloss>all-base consciousness</gloss> are completely exhausted. The consciousnesses that appear as the environment, the body, and enjoyments are ceased. Having discarded the characteristics of the all-base consciousness, one fully adopts the characteristics of the stainless realm. That very stainless realm is the <term>kaya</term> <gloss>body</gloss> of the Buddhas. Upon attaining that, and by relying on it in such a way, one attains the <term>sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>complete enjoyment body</gloss> and the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>; such is the established tenet.

According to this tenet, the Perfection of Wisdom itself should be meditated upon for the sake of Buddhahood. This is because, through the division of two types of meaning, it is the primordial wisdom that is truly without entities, determined to be without duality. Through this, the false aspects of duality subside, and there is an appearance of mere clarity that is infinite.

If one thinks: "In that case, the meditation on the forms of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>a semi-wrathful male deity</gloss> and the <term>Yoginis</term> <gloss>female deities</gloss>, along with mantras, signs, seats, celestial palaces, and so forth, involves conceptual elaboration and is erroneous; it gives rise to the cycle of afflictions and is not the source of liberation," then, in order to clarify that, it is said: "Liberation is through the very nature of entities." Here, "entity" refers to that which establishes one most firmly and is intended to mean "that which causes one to thoroughly obtain all the qualities of a Buddha."

One endowed with great compassion is liberated by the six perfections themselves; for that reason, they are addressed as "Great Compassionate One." One who is liberated by the Perfection of Wisdom alone quickly abandons the afflictions and becomes an <term>Arhat</term> <gloss>one who has overcome the inner enemies</gloss>. Therefore, such a person progresses specifically toward the enlightenment of a <term>Sravaka</term> <gloss>Hearer</gloss>, but not toward the enlightenment of a Buddha. A <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>hero of enlightenment</gloss> endowed with great compassion accomplishes the supreme benefit of sentient beings and aspires toward unexcelled enlightenment, not toward the lower state. Furthermore, they are liberated by the six perfections themselves, not by one alone. If they are liberated by the six, then what is the function of the first five, and what does the sixth perform?

Is it not so? This refers to that which is <term>false</term> <gloss>Tibetan: rdzun pa</gloss>. Because the great elements and so forth are conceptually constructed by mistaken consciousness, they lack any inherent essence of their own. Therefore, they dissolve into non-mistaken <term>primordial wisdom</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: jñāna</gloss>. On this point, it is excellent that the <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Middle Way school</gloss> and the <term>Yogacara</term> <gloss>Practitioners of Yoga school</gloss> share the same established conclusion: everything does not exist in a dualistic manner, yet everything is not non-existent in the manner of mere clarity without duality. Other views, such as the three Madhyamaka positions and the four Yogacara positions, have already been refuted by those learned in valid cognition, scripture, and treatises.

Furthermore, if one asks how this great primordial wisdom is <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>The Joyful Vajra</gloss>, it is because its nature is great wisdom and great compassion. From what does this arise? It arises from the nature of accomplishing the benefit of all beings for all time, and the nature of what is to be attained by meditating on the qualities of a Buddha and the qualities of a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>one intent on enlightenment</gloss>, for it is the very vessel of those qualities.

If that is the case, and if that is the <term>causal continuum</term> <gloss>Tibetan: rgyu'i rgyud</gloss>, then how can it be called the <term>method continuum</term> <gloss>Tibetan: thabs kyi rgyud</gloss>? This is true because it functions as the blessing of the body, as all-pervading mere clarity, as that which illuminates, as great bliss, as the vessel for the qualities of the Buddhas, and as the synthesis of the entire <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>. If one constantly brings this to mind, all the <term>Tathagatas</term> <gloss>Buddhas; literally "Thus-Gone Ones"</gloss> grant their blessing. Here, the method continuum is primary; because the act of mental engagement and the object of mental engagement appear as one, inseparably, that very state is the method continuum.

For the purpose of meditating on this great primordial wisdom, the blessing of all its <term>mudras</term> <gloss>ritual gestures or seals</gloss> is as follows: the subtle <term>hum</term> syllable without remainder, the vowels, the moon, and the absence of the <term>bindu</term> <gloss>drop or point</gloss>; or the subtle bindu the size of a mustard seed; or the supreme subtlety; or the placement of the four syllables according to the division of the four <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss>. 

If one objects that this aspect of the mudra belongs to the <term>generation stage</term> <gloss>Tibetan: bskyed rim</gloss> and not the <term>completion stage</term> <gloss>Tibetan: rdzogs rim</gloss>, that is not so. In this context, the term "generation stage" is used according to its worldly renown <unclear>text continues</unclear>

Both nostrils are the gateways. Regarding the sixteen shifts <note>original: "འཕོ་བ་" <gloss>transference or shifting of the breath</gloss></note>, the breath flows through these two nostrils for half a session <term>thun</term> <gloss>a period of three hours</gloss> each. This results in sixteen shifts throughout a full day and night. The sixty-four sticks <term>dbyu gu</term> <gloss>a measure of time equal to 22.5 minutes</gloss> refer to the duration of a full day and night. Two sticks constitute one water-clock measure <term>chu tshod</term> <gloss>24 minutes in this context, though often used interchangeably with dbyu gu</gloss>. There are thirty-two water-clock measures in a full day and night. A quarter of a session is one water-clock measure. The four sessions refer to either the day or the night; thus, there are eight sessions in a full twenty-four-hour day. Regarding this, the verse says:

There are four sessions in the night and four in the day;
A quarter of one session is a water-clock measure.
Two sticks make one water-clock measure.
The breath moves in and out through the two nostrils.
Six breaths make one life-breath <term>srog</term> <gloss>prana or respiration unit</gloss>.
That life-breath consists of fifty units,
Along with three and three-quarters breaths.
By moving to the North and South <note>referring to the solar and lunar shifts of the breath</note>,
During the first cycles of day and night.
Thus, the day and night increase or decrease,
Until the first movement of the other.
Likewise, whatever occurs in day and night,
The daily decrease is measured by the stick.
Breaths including a quarter of the fierce <note>referring to a specific rhythmic calculation</note>,
In the increase and decrease of each shift,
Breaths of a third, a quarter, or a sixth part,
Are what constitute the day and the night.

In this way, the shifting of the <term>mandala</term> <gloss>the elemental cycles of the breath</gloss> is illustrated by the movement of the wind through the two channels. As stated in the Union <term>kha sbyor</term> <gloss>the Samputa Tantra</gloss>:

By fire, wind,
The Great Powerful One <note>the element earth</note>, and water,
The breath flows everywhere within that mandala.
Upward, stacked, horizontal, and downward.
The Great Powerful One becomes the king.
Through water, purposes are perfectly accomplished.
Through fire, death occurs.
Through wind, wealth is exhausted.

There are many such explanations, but I shall leave them aside for fear of being too wordy <note>original: "ཚིག་མངས་སུ་དོགས་པས་"</note>. I shall now explain the six types of mindfulness regarding the exhaling and inhaling of the breath. To stabilize the mind, one must gain victory over the wind. As stated in the Abhidharma:

Counting, following, and placing,
Observing characteristics, then returning,
And total purification; these are the six.
They are held to be the mindfulness of inhaling and exhaling.

In this context, "entering" refers to the inhalation, which is the incoming wind. "Exiting" refers to...

It is known. Above that, one should visualize the garland of thirty-four consonants starting with <term>Ka</term> <gloss>the first letter of the Tibetan/Sanskrit alphabet</gloss> in the same manner, transforming into the disk of the sun. This transformation of the <term>Kali</term> <gloss>the series of consonants</gloss> into the sun is the sun of the <term>Kali</term>; it is the Wisdom of Equality <note>original: "mnyam pa nyid kྱི་ ye shes", Sanskrit: samatājñāna</note>. Regarding the phrase, "the seed residing in the center," it means residing in the center of the sun. On top of the center of the sun, a blue vajra born from the seed syllable resides there. This is the meaning of the phrase, "the seed resides in the center of the navel." This very seed, transformed into the form of the syllable <term>Hum</term>, is called the "Being" <note>original: "sems dpa'", Sanskrit: sattva</note>. This means that which is born as the seed is called Vajrasattva. If one asks what its nature is, it is of the nature of supreme bliss, the nature of Method and Wisdom. From the union of the <term>Ali</term> <gloss>the series of vowels</gloss> as the moon and the <term>Kali</term> as the sun, there arise three divisions of the nature of Great Bliss: the union, the actual state, and the conclusion. This is the Wisdom of Discernment <note>original: "so sor rtog pa'i ye shes", Sanskrit: pratyavekṣaṇajñāna</note>. Regarding "emanating forth," it refers to emanating from that very seed of one's own. If one asks what is emanated, it is "one's own likeness," such as the body of Hevajra. It is the condensed form of all the deities of the mantra, blue in color, possessing a wrathful expression, appearing in the forms of the fifteen yoginis as a method to subdue all beings, adorning and covering the sphere of the sky. Regarding "should be withdrawn into the heart," all those forms of the deities are to be withdrawn and dissolved into that very seed syllable. The unification of all these into the seed of one's own mantra is the All-Accomplishing Wisdom <note>original: "bya ba grub pa'i ye shes", Sanskrit: kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna</note>. Then, the phrase "the yogi becomes the nature of hatred" <note>In the context of the five buddha families, hatred/anger is the transformed emotion associated with the Akshobhya/Vajra family to which Hevajra belongs</note> means that after the moon, sun, vajra, and seed have completely transformed, one attains the body of Hevajra with the colors, ornaments, expressions, and marks that will be described. These are the Wisdom of the Dharmadhatu <note>original: "chos kyi dbyings kyi ye shes", Sanskrit: dharmadhātujñāna</note> which is utterly pure. By the transformation of the support, one finds Great Enlightenment in its distinguished essence. Thus, the awakening through the five wisdoms such as the Mirror-like Wisdom is the Awakening in Five Aspects. This will be explained in the eighth chapter: "The moon possesses the Mirror-like Wisdom; the Seven-Horsed One <gloss>the sun</gloss> is Equality; one's own deity..."

The seed syllables and hand symbols are explained as the <term>discernment</term> <gloss>the wisdom of individual investigation</gloss>. One should strive to unify all things. This is the perfection of the purity of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>the sphere of ultimate reality</gloss>. The learned ones have taught that these five aspects should be meditated upon.

Regarding the statement that one becomes the nature of hatred: hatred here refers to <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the Joyful Vajra</gloss>. What is he like? He has a complexion that appears blue and red. The phrase "or Great Black One" <note>original: "Mahakala"</note> is a supplementary description. "Red Bandhu" refers to his red eyes; thus he is the one with eyes like the red <term>Bandhujivaka</term> flower. The mass of his hair is orange and bristles upward; this is what is meant by the description of his hair.

"With the five seals" refers to the ornaments of the <term>mudras</term> <gloss>ritual hand gestures or symbolic ornaments</gloss>. A skull marked by a <term>vajra</term> <gloss>ritual thunderbolt</gloss> is a vajra-skull. "He holds it" is a supplementary phrase. "Having the nature of expression" refers to the manner of expression. These three points demonstrate the practice of the solitary hero <note>a meditation on a single deity without a consort or retinue</note>.

Speaking in terms of the fourth yoga, regarding the phrase "charnel ground" and so forth, there are five stages of yoga: <term>shamatha</term> <gloss>calm abiding</gloss>, <term>vipashyana</term> <gloss>insight</gloss>, the cultivation of both, and the delight in both, which is the view. The seal of this delight is the "play" that prevents distraction. Therefore, it is called "play." The "eight" refers to <term>Gauri</term> and the other goddesses. Just as there are branches for the third yoga, so it is for the fourth.

As for the body of the yoga: after visualizing the eight charnel grounds and so forth in the cardinal and intermediate directions within the four walls, one should meditate on the two stages of the mandala of the seat which will be explained in the center. In the middle of that, just as the three types of meditative absorption of the sixteen-armed glorious <term>Heruka</term> will be explained, one should meditate on the two-armed form. This is the fourth application of the Blessed One surrounded by the eight <term>yoginis</term>, and not the solitary hero. Why does he play in the charnel ground? Regarding the phrase "charnel ground" and so forth, the teaching of one word implies the application of others. For example, the name "Terrifier" <note>original: "Bhairava"</note> implies the class of terrifiers; if "not" is mentioned, it implies "immortal"; if "U" is mentioned, it implies "U, the Lord."

I am the mundane world as well. Just as I am the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss>, which is the natural result of the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of Great Bliss, I am also the world that serves as the natural result of the Great Bliss of the father, the mother, and the sentient beings of the intermediate state. I am also the <term>gandharva</term> <gloss>scent-eater/intermediate state being</gloss> who is swooning with Great Bliss.

If one asks: "How is that which is mundane Great Bliss the primary object of meditation?" 

It is said: "That which is called Sahaja-ananda <gloss>Co-emergent Joy</gloss>," and so forth. 

"Well then, if You are the primary Great Bliss to be accomplished, and the co-emergent joy of cyclic existence is not the object of accomplishment, why are You the primary object of accomplishment?"

It is said: "If that is the case, then 'I'..." and so forth. The word "also" implies the cause; because that very thing, in that way, causes the primary one to be trusted. One establishes the realization through a corresponding example; therefore, that very thing is designated as "I, the primary one."

"Like a lamp in the darkness." This means that just as a lamp makes one clearly perceive a vase or other objects in a dark room, the Co-emergent Joy of the example makes the Bliss that is the object of accomplishment clear.

"I dwell in Sukhavati <gloss>The Blissful Realm</gloss>," and so forth. To clarify those words, it is said: "The Teacher of the thirty..." and so forth. The primary aspect is the enjoyment of the Doctrine with the Bodhisattvas born in that body blazing with the major and minor marks of a Buddha. It means: "A self such as this dwells in Sukhavati."

The "Consort" refers to the <term>Vajra Consort</term> <gloss>the wisdom partner</gloss> and the "Example Consort" <gloss>the physical partner</gloss>. I dwell in their <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> in the form of the "fluid." The "fluid" refers to the seed of primordial wisdom and the external seed of the example. That is what is called "fluid."

Therefore, Great Bliss is that which depends upon the perfect union of the seed, the body, and the speech. Without that, since it does not arise from any other cause, one must generate bliss from the body of divine union. Consequently, those who seek the Bliss that is the object of accomplishment must certainly meditate on the <term>Deity Yoga</term>. This is the intended meaning.

<summary>This page explains the tantric principle of using mundane co-emergent joy as a pedagogical example to realize the ultimate Great Bliss of a Buddha. It identifies the practitioner's enlightened potential with the "fluid" or "seed" within the union of method and wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Great Bliss, Sahaja, Sukhavati, Sambhogakaya, Deity Yoga, Consort, Seed, Co-emergent Joy</keywords>

The syllable <term>Ba</term> <gloss>the second syllable of the name Varahi</gloss> refers to the melting of the moon <note>referring to the lunar essence or white bodhicitta</note>. All of this is explained in detail in the eighth chapter. Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>Vow or Binding</gloss>?" which was not explained previously, these are additional words forming a question. "Please explain" is the request being made. If one asks what was commanded in response, the answer begins with the phrase "The one called the Yogini."

"In the center of the body" refers to the navel. <term>A</term> is the first vowel. "Abiding" means it dwells there eternally. "Yogini" refers to <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>She Who is Without Self</gloss>, and this is connected to the term <term>Samvara</term>.

The meaning of the word <term>Samvara</term> is then explained. The phrase "Just as it is..." and so forth means that just as it is in the external world, so too should it be viewed internally; the internal is not inferior to the external. Regarding the statement "I do not perceive any phenomenon that attains complete enlightenment, nor any phenomenon by which one attains complete enlightenment," this means that although I understand all phenomena in every aspect through conventional knowledge subsumed under the wisdom of omniscience, when analyzed by ultimate wisdom, I do not see any subject that knows or any phenomenon to be known, just like objects seen in a dream.

The phrase "O sons of the gods, it is because all phenomena are utterly pure" refers here to the fact that non-existence itself is called purity. This is a synonym for being utterly non-existent.

The statement "O Blessed One, it is not difficult to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" is made because all phenomena are non-existent. It is not difficult to realize that a non-existent thing is non-existent. It would be difficult to realize the true nature of phenomena if they actually existed. It is not difficult to know and accomplish the practice by simply knowing that what is non-existent is non-existent. If phenomena were existent, one would need to accomplish practices such as the <term>paramitas</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> in order to increase virtuous qualities and abandon non-virtuous qualities. However, because these phenomena do not exist, the accomplishment is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that "attaining complete enlightenment is not difficult."

The intention behind the Elder Shariputra’s statement that attaining complete enlightenment is difficult is as follows: If it were enough to simply remain in silence after realizing that all phenomena are non-existent in nature, like space, then it would not be difficult. However, one must realize that in reality there is no such thing as attaining complete enlightenment regarding any phenomenon, and yet, following that, one must still engage in the practices of the perfections and completely realize all phenomena.

It was composed to correctly show the method for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment to those who are confused about it, to cause those who are heedless to correctly adopt it, to correctly encourage those who are discouraged, and to cause those who have correctly entered the path to be truly joyful.

The number four is mentioned to set aside the reluctance of those who might not wish to listen out of fear that the teachings are too vast. By mentioning the number, they are easily remembered. How is it through application? It is because one strives for the sake of one's own unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of completely protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to confess this. If this is true, I now ask you whether the poison should not be separated from the good and useful? And the good taken, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If therefore it must be so, I pray you, tell me how it is separated in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into confessing that poison lies hidden there, and are asked where it finally goes: then you bring forth I know not what about "corrections" which are said to drive out and take away the poison, <margin>The correction of Physicians is examined.</margin> just as they "correct" <term>Scammony</term> <gloss>a harsh purgative resin</gloss> with Quince, and afterwards call it <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a prepared form of scammony</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>an East Indian root used as a purgative</gloss>, and call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make the danger by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. <margin>What it is to "Correct" for a Physician.</margin> *To correct is to take what is already corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; the power lies within the things themselves, not within you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that a similar separation is necessary. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained.

Now therefore, at last, if that true foundation which removes poison is required, let us see how Alchemy performs it. For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if <term>Mars</term> <gloss>Iron/Antimony</gloss> is in the <term>Sun</term> <gloss>Gold</gloss>, Mars is removed; and if <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> is turned into <term>Venus</term> <gloss>Copper</gloss>, it is separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But those bodies which are contrary, it is entirely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is taken away from the good which you seek. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so a Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into another generation, which ought to benefit and help man. And should this not deservedly be judged the upright foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but rather <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret remedies</gloss>. <margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin> However, all those preparations of the workshops, as many as there are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine; but they are simply occupied in "correcting," as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell, is it therefore lawful for anyone to say the stench is separated and no longer remains? Indeed it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus, therefore, the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt <term>Aleopaticum</term> <note>likely a reference to a bitter aloes-based compound</note> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. What else, I ask, can they boast about their remedies, except to say, *This Electuary is sweet, made of spices and sugar,*

There is, therefore, in all metals a true Mercury and a right sulfur, equally in the imperfect as in the perfect metals.
